config.title: Human Computer Interaction
config.description: Master Human-Computer Interaction lectures (Usability, Interaction Paradigms, Display Design, UX Psychology, and Gestalt) and Video frameworks (5 Elements of UX and 7 UX Attributes).

questions.question: What is the primary goal of Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) when designing, evaluating, and implementing interactive computing systems?

options.label: A
options.text: Maximizing raw hardware clock speed and minimizing manufacturing cost

options.label: B
options.text: Making interactive systems usable, efficient, and satisfying for users

options.label: C
options.text: Replacing all human decision-making with autonomous batch scripts

options.label: D
options.text: Increasing screen pixel density regardless of user task workflows

questions.explanation: HCI studies how people interact with computer-based systems to make those interactions smooth, usable, efficient, and satisfying for the user.
questions.hint: Think about an everyday system like an ATM: what qualities make your interaction with it successful rather than frustrating?

questions.question: How do User Interface (UI) and User Experience (UX) fundamentally differ according to the course lectures?

options.label: A
options.text: UI is the visual look, feel, and direct interaction components, whereas UX encompasses the overall experience, emotions, and satisfaction of using the product

options.label: B
options.text: UX refers strictly to screen colors and typography, whereas UI refers only to backend database architecture

options.label: C
options.text: UI applies only to mobile apps, whereas UX applies only to desktop websites

options.label: D
options.text: They are completely identical terms that only cover how fast a user can type commands

questions.explanation: UI is the specific point of direct interaction (menus, buttons, layout, visual look and feel), while UX is the broader, holistic experience including usability, aesthetics, emotions, and enjoyment.
questions.hint: Which term describes the concrete screen controls you touch, and which describes how the entire journey makes you feel?

questions.question: Imagine an ATM where pressing the button labeled Next unexpectedly takes the user backward to the previous screen. Which core HCI concept does this design flaw directly violate?

options.label: A
options.text: Batch Processing

options.label: B
options.text: User's Mental Model

options.label: C
options.text: Visual Angle Formula

options.label: D
options.text: Brain-Computer Interface

questions.explanation: A mental model is the user's internal representation of how a system works based on prior experience. Having 'Next' go backward clashes with the user's mental model and causes immediate confusion.
questions.hint: What internal picture do users carry in their heads about how familiar controls like 'Next' or swiping should behave?

questions.question: Which field specifically applies psychological principles to understand how users process information and make decisions—for example, recommending larger fonts for critical alerts to reduce strain?

options.label: A
options.text: Cognitive Ergonomics

options.label: B
options.text: Network Topology

options.label: C
options.text: Batch Scheduling

options.label: D
options.text: Hardware Overclocking

questions.explanation: Cognitive ergonomics studies human information processing and decision-making so interactive systems can be designed to reduce cognitive strain and human error.
questions.hint: Which discipline bridges human mental processing ('cognitive') with designing comfortable, strain-free systems ('ergonomics')?

questions.question:
In HCI, how does Interaction Design differ from Information Architecture (IA)?
DisciplinePrimary Focus
Interaction Design?
Information Architecture?

options.label: A
options.text: Interaction Design plans the sequence of steps and flow of user-system action; IA organizes, categorizes, and labels information like a library

options.label: B
options.text: Interaction Design categorizes news articles; IA writes backend SQL queries

options.label: C
options.text: Interaction Design tests hardware durability; IA measures screen brightness

options.label: D
options.text: Interaction Design only creates static logos; IA only designs audio alerts

questions.explanation: Interaction Design focuses on the flow and sequence of steps a user takes to achieve a goal, whereas Information Architecture (IA) focuses on organizing, categorizing, and labeling content so users can find what they need.
questions.hint: If one is like a library's cataloging system and the other is like a guided multi-step workflow, how do their roles map?

questions.question: Which HCI methodology requires observing real users via usability testing, surveys, or eye-tracking to measure performance and identify pain points?

options.label: A
options.text: Empirical measurement / Evaluation

options.label: B
options.text: Task elimination

options.label: C
options.text: Unverified aesthetic speculation

options.label: D
options.text: Batch compilation

questions.explanation: Evaluation (and empirical measurement) assesses a system's usability by observing real users, measuring performance, and uncovering pain points for iterative improvement.
questions.hint: How do designers verify whether a system actually works for real people rather than just guessing?

questions.question: A cluttered user interface (UI) improves task efficiency because placing competing elements and heavy decorative styling on a single screen lowers the user's cognitive load.

options.label: A
options.text: True

options.label: B
options.text: False

questions.explanation: False. A cluttered UI features too many competing elements, unclear structures, or unnecessary styling, which overwhelms users and significantly increases cognitive load.
questions.hint: When too many visual elements compete for your attention at once, does your brain work harder or less hard?

questions.question: Review the 7 core usability design principles from the lecture diagram. Which principle specifically means "make usage obvious" so the user immediately knows how an object or control can be operated?
questions.diagram:
mindmap
  root((7 Design Principles))
    Tolerance
    Simplicity
    Visibility
    Affordance
    Consistency
    Structure
    Feedback

options.label: A
options.text: Tolerance

options.label: B
options.text: Affordance

options.label: C
options.text: Feedback

options.label: D
options.text: Structure

questions.explanation: Affordance means making usage obvious—designing a control (such as a raised button or a slider handle) so its visual properties naturally suggest how to interact with it.
questions.hint: Which term describes a visual clue on an object (like a door handle or a 3D button) that naturally invites pushing, pulling, or clicking?

questions.question: Among the 7 usability design principles, what is the role of Tolerance?

options.label: A
options.text: Error prevention and recovery—helping users avoid mistakes and easily undo or recover when errors occur

options.label: B
options.text: Showing the visual results of an action after a button is clicked

options.label: C
options.text: Using the exact same visual pattern on every page

options.label: D
options.text: Organizing information into logical categories

questions.explanation: Tolerance refers to error prevention and recovery: designing flexible interfaces that prevent user mistakes where possible and provide safe recovery paths (like Undo or clear confirmation prompts).
questions.hint: What does it mean for a system to be 'forgiving' or 'tolerant' when a human inevitably makes a mistake?

questions.question: When a user clicks a 'Submit' button and the button immediately displays a spinning loader followed by a green checkmark, which of the 7 usability principles is directly demonstrated?

options.label: A
options.text: Feedback (show results of action)

options.label: B
options.text: Structure (organize info logically)

options.label: C
options.text: Simplicity

options.label: D
options.text: Tolerance

questions.explanation: Feedback informs the user about what the system is doing and shows the immediate result of their action.
questions.hint: How does the system communicate back to you that your click actually registered?

questions.question: Besides Usability, the lecture highlights three additional pillars that shape effective HCI systems: Context, Accessibility, and Goal-Oriented design. Which scenario best illustrates designing for Context?

options.label: A
options.text: Adapting an automotive navigation display for high-glare, hands-busy driving conditions rather than a quiet office desk

options.label: B
options.text: Removing all user goals from the requirements document

options.label: C
options.text: Requiring every user to memorize command-line flags

options.label: D
options.text: Using identical tiny 8pt text on both smartwatches and highway billboards

questions.explanation: Designing for Context means accounting for the physical, social, and environmental conditions in which the user actually operates the system.
questions.hint: Why would an interface that works great in a quiet bedroom fail when used by a driver on a sunny highway?

questions.question: Which historical HCI interaction paradigm involves submitting a complete set of instructions (such as punched cards on early mainframes) and waiting for sequential execution with no real-time interaction?
questions.diagram:
timeline
    title Evolution of Interaction Paradigms
    Early Mainframes : Batch Processing
    Text Terminals : Command-Line Interface (CLI)
    Desktop Era : GUI & Direct Manipulation
    Modern Era : Ubiquitous, AR/VR & BCI

options.label: A
options.text: Batch Processing Paradigm

options.label: B
options.text: Event-Driven Interaction Paradigm

options.label: C
options.text: Direct Manipulation Paradigm

options.label: D
options.text: Conversational Paradigm

questions.explanation: In the Batch Processing paradigm, users submit batch jobs for execution and wait for the output without any real-time interactive intervention.
questions.hint: Which paradigm processes jobs in 'batches' from start to finish without letting the user intervene mid-run?

questions.question: What is the primary trade-off between a Command-Line Interface (CLI) and a Menu-Driven Interaction Paradigm?

options.label: A
options.text: CLI offers powerful control but requires memorizing command syntax, whereas Menu-Driven interfaces present predefined options that reduce memory load

options.label: B
options.text: CLI requires no syntax knowledge, whereas Menu-Driven interfaces require typing Unix shell scripts

options.label: C
options.text: Menu-Driven interfaces only work with neural implants, whereas CLI only works on ATMs

options.label: D
options.text: Both paradigms prohibit real-time user input

questions.explanation: CLI (e.g., Linux shell, DOS) gives expert users powerful control at the cost of memorizing syntax, while Menu-Driven interfaces (e.g., ATMs, setup wizards) let users choose from predefined options without memorization.
questions.hint: Compare typing commands into a Linux terminal versus picking withdrawal options on an ATM screen—what does each demand from your memory?

questions.question: In photo-editing software, a user grabs a corner handle of an image and drags it to resize and rotate the picture with continuous, real-time visual feedback. Which interaction paradigm does this best exemplify?

options.label: A
options.text: Direct Manipulation Paradigm

options.label: B
options.text: Batch Processing Paradigm

options.label: C
options.text: Form-Fill Interaction Paradigm

options.label: D
options.text: Command-Line Interface Paradigm

questions.explanation: Direct Manipulation allows users to interact with digital objects as if they were physical entities, featuring intuitive actions like dragging/dropping and immediate real-time visual feedback.
questions.hint: When you grab, drag, and stretch a digital image as though holding a physical photo in your hands, what kind of manipulation is that?

questions.question: How do the Graphical User Interface (GUI) and Event-Driven Interaction paradigms relate to one another?

options.label: A
options.text: GUI provides visual elements (windows, icons, buttons), and it relies heavily on Event-Driven interaction where discrete user actions (clicks, keypresses) trigger system responses

options.label: B
options.text: Event-Driven systems execute only via punched cards and cannot use visual buttons

options.label: C
options.text: GUI systems ignore user clicks and run strictly on timed batch schedules

options.label: D
options.text: They are mutually exclusive paradigms that can never coexist in a web browser

questions.explanation: GUIs present visual components (windows, icons, menus, buttons), while the Event-Driven paradigm underpins how user actions (clicking a hyperlink, dragging) trigger corresponding system responses.
questions.hint: In a web browser (a GUI), what causes the system to load a new page when you click a link?

questions.question: An online banking registration page or digital survey that guides users to enter data into structured fields to standardize input and reduce errors is an example of which paradigm?

options.label: A
options.text: Form-Fill Interaction Paradigm

options.label: B
options.text: Tangible User Interface (TUI) Paradigm

options.label: C
options.text: Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) Paradigm

options.label: D
options.text: Ubiquitous Computing Paradigm

questions.explanation: The Form-Fill Interaction Paradigm uses structured forms for data entry, which standardizes user input and minimizes data entry errors.
questions.hint: Which paradigm mirrors filling out structured blanks on a paper form?

questions.question: Carefully distinguish between Ubiquitous (Pervasive) Computing and a Tangible User Interface (TUI):

options.label: A
options.text: Ubiquitous computing embeds invisible, context-aware computing into everyday environments (e.g., smart lighting reacting to occupancy), whereas TUI uses physical objects that users directly manipulate to control a digital display (e.g., museum exhibit blocks)

options.label: B
options.text: Ubiquitous computing requires typing DOS commands, whereas TUI requires wearing a VR headset

options.label: C
options.text: TUI is completely invisible with no physical objects, whereas Ubiquitous computing only exists on desktop monitors

options.label: D
options.text: Both refer exclusively to voice-only chatbots like Siri

questions.explanation: Ubiquitous (pervasive) computing focuses on seamless, invisible, context-aware systems embedded in the environment (like smart home lighting), while TUIs let users manipulate physical objects to control digital representations.
questions.hint: Which one happens seamlessly in the background of a smart room, and which one gives you a physical artifact to pick up and move to control a digital screen?

questions.question: Virtual assistants like Siri and Alexa, as well as AI chatbots that interact with users via natural language text or speech, belong to which interaction paradigm?

options.label: A
options.text: Conversational Paradigm

options.label: B
options.text: Batch Processing Paradigm

options.label: C
options.text: Form-Fill Paradigm

options.label: D
options.text: Tangible User Interface Paradigm

questions.explanation: The Conversational Paradigm enables users to interact with systems using natural language (speech or text) through context-aware dialogue.
questions.hint: When you talk or chat with an assistant in plain sentences, what kind of human interaction are you having?

questions.question: A furniture shopping app that overlays a 3D digital sofa onto your live smartphone camera view of your real living room alongside fully immersive 3D flight simulators represents which paradigm?

options.label: A
options.text: Augmented Reality (AR) & Virtual Reality (VR) Paradigm

options.label: B
options.text: Command-Line Interface (CLI) Paradigm

options.label: C
options.text: Menu-Driven Paradigm

options.label: D
options.text: Batch Processing Paradigm

questions.explanation: The AR & VR paradigm either overlays digital information onto the real world (AR) or places users inside immersive 3D environments (VR).
questions.hint: Which paradigm blends 3D digital overlays with the real world or immerses you in a virtual 3D space?

questions.question: Which interaction paradigm enables users to control prosthetic limbs or assistive communication systems directly via neural/brain signals without physical movement?

options.label: A
options.text: Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) Paradigm

options.label: B
options.text: Direct Manipulation Paradigm

options.label: C
options.text: Tangible User Interface (TUI) Paradigm

options.label: D
options.text: Event-Driven Mouse Paradigm

questions.explanation: Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs) translate brain signals directly into system commands without requiring physical muscle movement, playing a vital role in medical and accessibility technologies.
questions.hint: Which interface bypasses hands and voice entirely by reading neural activity directly?

questions.question: According to the Interaction Paradigms lecture, a single paradigm is universally superior for every task regardless of usability, efficiency, computing environment, or user preference.

options.label: A
options.text: True

options.label: B
options.text: False

questions.explanation: False. The choice of interaction paradigm depends on usability, efficiency, user needs, and computing environment, and paradigms evolve alongside technology.
questions.hint: Would a neural implant or a VR headset be the best choice for quickly entering a tax form, or does the best paradigm depend on the task and user?

questions.question: What are the four major categories into which the Thirteen Principles of Display Design are organized?
questions.diagram:
graph TD
    A[13 Principles of Display Design] --> B[1. Perceptual Principles]
    A --> C[2. Mental Model Principles]
    A --> D[3. Principles Based on Attention]
    A --> E[4. Memory Principles]

options.label: A
options.text: Perceptual Principles, Mental Model Principles, Principles Based on Attention, and Memory Principles

options.label: B
options.text: Hardware Principles, Network Principles, Database Principles, and Compiler Principles

options.label: C
options.text: Marketing Principles, Pricing Principles, Legal Principles, and Sales Principles

options.label: D
options.text: Batch Principles, CLI Principles, TUI Principles, and BCI Principles

questions.explanation: The 13 Principles of Display Design are grouped according to human information processing stages: Perceptual, Mental Model, Attention-based, and Memory principles.
questions.hint: Think about the human mind interacting with a display: how we see it, how we model it, how we focus on it, and how we remember it.

questions.question: Under the first Perceptual Principle (Make displays legible), why do aviation and medical device designers use the Visual Angle formula?

options.label: A
options.text: Because if the visual angle is too small for the viewing distance, the operator physically cannot distinguish the characters no matter how hard they concentrate

options.label: B
options.text: To calculate how many colors a monitor GPU can render per second

options.label: C
options.text: To encrypt sensitive medical data on the screen

options.label: D
options.text: To replace visual displays with audio-only alarms

questions.explanation: Legibility is a physical prerequisite of perception: if the visual angle subtended by characters at the operator's eye is below threshold, no amount of mental concentration can make them readable.
questions.hint: Can willpower alone allow a pilot to read tiny text from across the cockpit if the physical size-to-distance ratio is too small?

questions.question: A dashboard designer uses 12 slightly different shades of blue to represent 12 severity levels, with no text labels or icons. Which Perceptual Principle does this violate?

options.label: A
options.text: Avoid absolute judgment limits

options.label: B
options.text: Principle of predictive aiding

options.label: C
options.text: Principle of the moving part

options.label: D
options.text: Minimizing information access cost

questions.explanation: 'Avoid absolute judgment limits' states that you should not require a user to judge the level of a variable based on a single sensory variable (like color, size, or loudness) containing many levels.
questions.hint: How accurately can a human eye identify which exact shade of blue out of 12 is on screen when viewed in isolation?

questions.question: Why does combining a red color, an octagonal shape, and the text "STOP" on an alert button improve user performance according to Perceptual Principles?

options.label: A
options.text: It achieves Redundancy Gain by presenting the same information in multiple ways (color + shape + text), so users understand faster and more accurately even if one cue is missed

options.label: B
options.text: It forces the user to rely on absolute judgment limits of a single variable

options.label: C
options.text: It increases information access cost to slow down the operator

options.label: D
options.text: It eliminates top-down processing completely

questions.explanation: Redundancy gain occurs when the same information is encoded across multiple visual dimensions (e.g., color + shape + text), improving speed and accuracy even under degraded viewing conditions or color blindness.
questions.hint: What happens to comprehension speed and reliability when three distinct visual cues all reinforce the exact same message?

questions.question: Compare thePerceptual Principle of Top-Down Processing with the Mental Model Principle of Pictorial Realism:

options.label: A
options.text: Top-down processing describes how the brain interprets stimuli and fills in gaps using prior knowledge and context, while Pictorial Realism states that displays should visually resemble the real-world objects/concepts they represent (like a trash bin icon)

options.label: B
options.text: Top-down processing only applies to sound, while Pictorial Realism only applies to touch

options.label: C
options.text: Both principles state that icons should be abstract geometric random shapes

options.label: D
options.text: Top-down processing forbids using real-world metaphors

questions.explanation: Top-down processing is the perceptual mechanism where users interpret data based on prior knowledge, expectations, and context; Pictorial Realism is the mental model principle of designing displays/icons to look like the real-world objects they represent.
questions.hint: How does your brain's expectation from past experience interact with an icon designed to look like a real physical object?

questions.question: In an email client, the Delete File and Send File buttons are placed side by side with identical blue rounded-rectangle styling and nearly identical labels. Users frequently click Delete by mistake. Which Perceptual Principle explains this error?

options.label: A
options.text: Similarity causes confusion

options.label: B
options.text: Redundancy gain

options.label: C
options.text: Principle of multiple resources

options.label: D
options.text: Principle of predictive aiding

questions.explanation: The principle 'Similarity causes confusion' warns that when distinct controls with very different actions share overly similar visual appearances, users are prone to action slips and confusion.
questions.hint: When two opposite actions look almost identical at a glance, why does the human eye mix them up?

questions.question: According to the Mental Model Principles of Display Design (specifically the Principle of the Moving Part / Motion), how should movement be used in an interface?

options.label: A
options.text: Use motion strategically (such as a moving progress bar during a download) to draw attention to status changes, because overuse of motion distracts and confuses users

options.label: B
options.text: Animate every icon and paragraph continuously so the screen feels lively

options.label: C
options.text: Never use moving elements under any circumstances because human vision ignores motion

options.label: D
options.text: Move buttons randomly while the user tries to click them

questions.explanation: Human perception is highly sensitive to motion, so moving parts (like a progress bar) help users detect changes or alerts quickly—but motion must be used strategically, not excessively, to avoid distraction.
questions.hint: Because our peripheral vision automatically snaps toward movement, what happens if only critical status updates move versus if everything on screen bounces?

questions.question: Examine the three Principles Based on Attention below. Which example correctly matches Minimizing Information Access Cost?
questions.diagram:
graph LR
    A[Attention Principles] --> B[Minimize Access Cost]
    A --> C[Proximity Compatibility]
    A --> D[Multiple Resources]

options.label: A
options.text: Placing frequently used commands like Save and Undo directly on the main toolbar or adding search auto-suggestions to reduce time and effort

options.label: B
options.text: Hiding the Save button inside four nested sub-menus so the screen looks blank

options.label: C
options.text: Playing a loud siren while flashing red lights in a car

options.label: D
options.text: Forecasting tomorrow's stock prices on a trend line

questions.explanation: Information access cost is the time and physical/mental effort needed to locate information. Toolbar shortcuts, dashboard summaries, and auto-suggestions minimize this cost.
questions.hint: How can a designer reduce the 'cost' (in eye movements, clicks, and seconds) of reaching a tool you use every minute?

questions.question: In an aircraft cockpit display, airspeed, altitude, and heading indicators are grouped closely together in one panel so pilots can integrate flight status rapidly. Which Attention-based Display Design principle is applied?

options.label: A
options.text: Proximity compatibility principle

options.label: B
options.text: Principle of multiple resources

options.label: C
options.text: Avoid absolute judgment limits

options.label: D
options.text: Principle of predictive aiding

questions.explanation: The Proximity Compatibility Principle states that related information that must be mentally integrated should be placed close together in space, while unrelated information should be kept apart.
questions.hint: When two pieces of data must be compared or combined in your head, where should they sit on the physical display?

questions.question: A car reversing system combines an auditory beeping sound with visual red flashing lights to alert the driver of an obstacle. Which Display Design principle explains why distributing alerts across sight and sound works better than overloading vision alone?

options.label: A
options.text: Principle of multiple resources

options.label: B
options.text: Principle of pictorial realism

options.label: C
options.text: Replace memory with visual information

options.label: D
options.text: Similarity causes confusion

questions.explanation: The Principle of Multiple Resources notes that humans process information across distinct sensory channels (visual, auditory, tactile); distributing information across channels avoids overloading a single channel.
questions.hint: When a driver's eyes are already busy watching mirrors, why is adding a sound alert across a second sensory channel so effective?

questions.question: Compare the three Memory Principles of Display Design. Which pair correctly matches Replace Memory with Visual Information and Principle of Predictive Aiding?

options.label: A
options.text: Replace Memory: auto-fill fields showing past entries so users don't have to recall them; Predictive Aiding: GPS navigation showing estimated arrival time and upcoming traffic delays

options.label: B
options.text: Replace Memory: hiding all menus so users memorize shortcuts; Predictive Aiding: keeping warning colors identical

options.label: C
options.text: Replace Memory: forecasting stock trend lines; Predictive Aiding: using a trash can icon

options.label: D
options.text: Both principles require users to memorize 15-digit codes in short-term memory

questions.explanation: 'Replace memory with visual information' offloads short-term memory by showing data directly on the display (e.g., auto-fill entries), while 'Predictive aiding' helps users anticipate future states (e.g., GPS traffic forecasts, aircraft flight-path projections).
questions.hint: Which principle saves you from having to remember the past, and which helps you anticipate the future before a problem occurs?

questions.question:
In Lec 6 (Psychology of UX), the instructor compares two HTML snippets for a navigation menu item:
1) <li><a href="#">Home</a></li>
2) <a href="#"><li>Home</li></a>
Why does making the entire <li> block clickable illustrate Fitts's Law?

options.label: A
options.text: Because Fitts's Law states that larger and closer targets require less precision and take less time to acquire, reducing errors from the speed-accuracy trade-off

options.label: B
options.text: Because Fitts's Law states that users can only hold 7 plus or minus 2 items in working memory

options.label: C
options.text: Because smaller clickable targets force users to read more carefully

options.label: D
options.text: Because Fitts's Law only measures server response time under 400ms

questions.explanation: Fitts's Law governs target acquisition: closer is faster, larger is faster, and there is a speed-accuracy trade-off. Wrapping the entire list item container as a clickable target enlarges the hit area so users can click faster with fewer errors.
questions.hint: Is it easier and faster to click just the tiny letters 'Home' or the entire padded menu box surrounding it?

questions.question: Why do competing AI chat platforms (such as ChatGPT, Claude, and DeepSeek) share a remarkably similar layout with a left sidebar for chat history and a bottom prompt input box?

options.label: A
options.text: Jakob's Law: users spend most of their time on other sites and prefer your site to work the same way as all the other sites they already know

options.label: B
options.text: Von Restorff Effect: making every interface identical causes one button to stand out

options.label: C
options.text: Tesler's Law: complexity can be completely deleted from a system

options.label: D
options.text: Peak-End Rule: users only remember the sidebar when closing the app

questions.explanation: Jakob's Law states that users transfer expectations built around familiar products to yours; adopting established layout conventions lets users focus on their tasks rather than learning a new interface.
questions.hint: Where do users form their expectations about how a new website or app should behave before they even open yours?

questions.question:
Match Hick's Law, Miller's Law, and Tesler's Law to their core UX implications:
LawUX Principle
Hick's LawDecision time increases with the number and complexity of choices
Miller's LawAverage person can keep ~7 (±2) items in working memory (chunking)
Tesler's Law?

options.label: A
options.text: Conservation of Complexity: every system has an inherent amount of complexity that cannot be removed, only shifted from the user to the system/designer

options.label: B
options.text: Be liberal in what you accept and conservative in what you send

options.label: C
options.text: Users judge an experience purely by its aesthetic color palette

options.label: D
options.text: Targets closer to the cursor take longer to click

questions.explanation: Tesler's Law (Law of Conservation of Complexity) states that every application has an inherent amount of irreducible complexity; designers should absorb that complexity in the system rather than forcing it onto the user.
questions.hint: If a task's underlying complexity cannot simply vanish into thin air, who should bear the burden—the human user or the software behind the scenes?

questions.question: Coined by internet pioneer Jon Postel, Postel's Law states: "Be liberal in what you accept, and conservative in what you send." How is this applied to UX input validation and forms?

options.label: A
options.text: Accept flexible user input formats (e.g., phone numbers with spaces, dashes, or parentheses) while formatting and outputting clean, standardized system feedback

options.label: B
options.text: Reject any user input that contains spaces and display raw stack traces to the user

options.label: C
options.text: Send unpredictable random outputs while accepting only binary numbers

options.label: D
options.text: Remove all password strength indicators and error messages

questions.explanation: Like a gracious host, Postel's Law in UX means accommodating varied human inputs gracefully (input validation, helpful error handling, clear password guidance) and returning consistent, predictable, clean system outputs.
questions.hint: Remember the lecture's 'gracious host' analogy: how should a form treat a user who types spaces or dashes in their phone number?

questions.question: On a SaaS pricing page with three subscription cards, the 'Pro (Recommended)' tier is highlighted with a vibrant accent border and badge while the other two cards are neutral grey. Which psychological law explains why users notice and remember the Pro tier first?

options.label: A
options.text: Von Restorff Effect (Isolation Effect)

options.label: B
options.text: Doherty Threshold

options.label: C
options.text: Postel's Law

options.label: D
options.text: Jakob's Law

questions.explanation: The Von Restorff Effect predicts that when multiple homogeneous objects are presented, the one that differs visually from the rest is most likely to be noticed and remembered.
questions.hint: When one item stands out visually in a row of otherwise identical items, why does it magnetize your attention?

questions.question: In Lec 6, Psychological Laws are divided into two groups: Behavior Change (7 laws) and Emotional Fulfillment (3 laws). Which three laws belong to the Emotional Fulfillment category?
questions.diagram:
graph TD
    A[Psychology of UX] --> B[Behavior Change: 7 Laws]
    A --> C[Emotional Fulfillment: 3 Laws]
    C --> D[Peak-End Rule]
    C --> E[Doherty Threshold]
    C --> F[Aesthetic-Usability Effect]

options.label: A
options.text: Peak-End Rule, Doherty Threshold, and Aesthetic-Usability Effect

options.label: B
options.text: Fitts's Law, Jakob's Law, and Hick's Law

options.label: C
options.text: Miller's Law, Tesler's Law, and Postel's Law

options.label: D
options.text: Law of Closure, Law of Proximity, and Law of Continuity

questions.explanation: The lecture categorizes Peak-End Rule, Doherty Threshold, and Aesthetic-Usability Effect under Emotional Fulfillment, whereas Fitts's, Jakob's, Hick's, Miller's, Tesler's, Postel's, and Von Restorff are under Behavior Change.
questions.hint: Which three laws focus on how users emotionally remember an experience, feel kept in flow via fast/placeholder feedback, and perceive attractive designs as more usable?

questions.question: Why did the Lec 6 slides reference Bootstrap Skeleton Placeholders when discussing the Doherty Threshold, and how does this differ from the Peak-End Rule and Aesthetic-Usability Effect?

options.label: A
options.text: Doherty Threshold requires system feedback within ~400ms (using skeleton placeholders to maintain perceived speed and engagement), whereas Peak-End judges an experience by its most intense point and final moment, and Aesthetic-Usability makes attractive designs seem easier to use

options.label: B
options.text: Doherty Threshold states that users only remember the last error message, whereas Peak-End requires 400ms server latency

options.label: C
options.text: Bootstrap placeholders intentionally slow down page rendering to test user patience

options.label: D
options.text: Aesthetic-Usability Effect means ugly interfaces always load under 400ms

questions.explanation: Productivity soars when computer and user interact at a pace (<400ms) where neither waits on the other (Doherty Threshold); skeleton placeholders maintain perceived responsiveness while content loads.
questions.hint: How do animated grey content placeholders keep your brain engaged during a brief load so the app still feels instantaneous?

questions.question: In the Gestalt perceptual hierarchy, suppose four identical circles are spaced equally in a row, but a line physically connects the first three circles while a box encloses two others. Which principle is the strongest among Gestalt principles, and which principle overrides Shape Similarity?

options.label: A
options.text: Law of Connectedness is the strongest overall principle, and Color is the strongest visual attribute Within Similarity (overriding Shape)

options.label: B
options.text: Shape Similarity is stronger than Connectedness, Common Region, and Proximity

options.label: C
options.text: Law of Closure always overrides Connectedness

options.label: D
options.text: All Gestalt laws have identical perceptual strength

questions.explanation: Connectedness (linking elements with explicit lines, as in checkout step diagrams or VS Code indent guides) is the strongest Gestalt grouping principle, while Common Region overrides Proximity, and Color overrides Shape in Similarity.
questions.hint: What happens to your perception when an explicit line physically ties elements together, or when one row of mixed shapes is given the same color?

questions.question:
Match each real-world UI design pattern to its corresponding Gestalt principle:
1) Instagram Stories showing a partial cut-off circle at the screen edge to signal scrollable stories
2) iOS App Library grouping apps inside distinct rounded background containers
3) iMessage blurring the background when replying to focus attention on the active message

options.label: A
options.text: 1 = Law of Closure, 2 = Law of Common Region, 3 = Law of Figure/Ground

options.label: B
options.text: 1 = Law of Common Fate, 2 = Law of Continuity, 3 = Law of Similarity

options.label: C
options.text: 1 = Law of Figure/Ground, 2 = Law of Closure, 3 = Law of Connectedness

options.label: D
options.text: 1 = Law of Proximity, 2 = Law of Common Fate, 3 = Law of Continuity

questions.explanation: A partial circle that the brain completes is Closure ( signifying more content off-screen); bounded containers are Common Region; separating the active focal message from a blurred background is Figure/Ground (like Rubin's Vase).
questions.hint: Which principle fills in missing pieces of a cut-off shape, which encloses items inside a border, and which separates foreground focus from background?

questions.question: How does the Law of Common Fate differ from the Law of Continuity in UI design?

options.label: A
options.text: Common Fate groups elements that move together in synchronized motion (e.g., carousel slides or coordinated dropdown transitions), whereas Continuity leads the eye along smooth, uninterrupted lines or grid alignments (e.g., form grids and flowcharts)

options.label: B
options.text: Common Fate only applies to static print menus, whereas Continuity only applies to sound effects

options.label: C
options.text: Continuity requires objects to flash randomly, whereas Common Fate forbids animation

options.label: D
options.text: They both refer strictly to changing font sizes

questions.explanation: Common Fate relies on synchronized movement (like a flock of birds, UI carousels, or animated dropdown menus), whereas Continuity relies on smooth, unbroken spatial paths and grid alignment.
questions.hint: Which principle is about synchronized *movement* in the same direction, and which is about following a smooth *path or alignment*?

questions.question: According to the 5 Elements of User Experience diagram from the video, what is the correct bottom-to-top order of the five planes (following the upward arrows from foundational to visible)?
questions.diagram:
graph BT
    S1[1. Strategy] --> S2[2. Scope]
    S2 --> S3[3. Structure]
    S3 --> S4[4. Skeleton]
    S4 --> S5[5. Surface]

options.label: A
options.text: Strategy → Scope → Structure → Skeleton → Surface

options.label: B
options.text: Surface → Skeleton → Structure → Scope → Strategy

options.label: C
options.text: Scope → Strategy → Skeleton → Structure → Surface

options.label: D
options.text: Strategy → Structure → Scope → Surface → Skeleton

questions.explanation: In the 5 Elements of User Experience framework, the planes build from bottom to top: Strategy (bottom) → Scope → Structure → Skeleton → Surface (top).
questions.hint: Start at the foundational 'why' at the very bottom of the diagram and move upward toward the visual screen at the top.

questions.question: In the 5 Elements of User Experience framework, which two components make up the foundational Strategy plane?

options.label: A
options.text: Business Goals and User Needs

options.label: B
options.text: Functional Specifications and Content Requirements

options.label: C
options.text: Interaction Design and Information Architecture

options.label: D
options.text: Interface Design and Navigation Design

questions.explanation: The Strategy plane sits at the base of the 5 Elements of UX and balances two core pillars: Business Goals (what the organization wants to achieve) and User Needs (what the users want to achieve).
questions.hint: Before deciding what features to build, whose two sets of goals and needs must a product strategy align?

questions.question: Which two components belong to the Scope plane (the second plane from the bottom in the 5 Elements of User Experience)?

options.label: A
options.text: Functional Specifications and Content Requirements

options.label: B
options.text: Business Goals and User Needs

options.label: C
options.text: Interface Design and Navigation Design

options.label: D
options.text: Visual Design and Typography

questions.explanation: Once Strategy is defined, the Scope plane translates it into what the product will include: Functional Specifications (features/functions) and Content Requirements (information/media).
questions.hint: When defining the 'scope' of a project, how do you specify what features the software will have and what content it will provide?

questions.question: In the 5 Elements of User Experience diagram, the middle plane is Structure. Which two disciplines form the Structure plane?

options.label: A
options.text: Interaction Design and Information Architecture

options.label: B
options.text: Functional Specifications and Content Requirements

options.label: C
options.text: Interface Design and Navigation Design

options.label: D
options.text: Business Goals and Visual Design

questions.explanation: The Structure plane defines how the features and content from the Scope plane fit together cohesively through Interaction Design and Information Architecture.
questions.hint: Which two disciplines organize how the system behaves in response to the user and how the information categories are structured?

questions.question: Sitting directly below Surface and above Structure is the Skeleton plane. Which two components are shown inside the Skeleton plane in the video overview?

options.label: A
options.text: Interface Design and Navigation Design

options.label: B
options.text: Interaction Design and Information Architecture

options.label: C
options.text: Functional Specifications and Content Requirements

options.label: D
options.text: Business Goals and User Needs

questions.explanation: In the video overview diagram, the Skeleton plane consists of Interface Design (arranging interface elements for interaction) and Navigation Design (allowing users to move through the information architecture).
questions.hint: Think of a wireframe 'skeleton': what designs the arrangement of screen controls and the pathways for moving between pages?

questions.question: At the very top of the 5 Elements of User Experience hierarchy sits the Surface plane (marked with an eye icon). What corresponds to the Surface plane?

options.label: A
options.text: Visual Design

options.label: B
options.text: Functional Specifications

options.label: C
options.text: Information Architecture

options.label: D
options.text: User Needs

questions.explanation: The Surface plane is represented by Visual Design—the sensory, visible appearance of the product (colors, typography, imagery) that users directly see first.
questions.hint: What is the top layer of a digital product that immediately meets the user's eye?

questions.question:
Examine the two columns of the 5 Elements of User Experience diagram from Strategy up to Skeleton:
PlaneLeft ColumnRight Column
SkeletonInterface DesignNavigation Design
StructureInteraction DesignInformation Architecture
ScopeFunctional SpecificationsContent Requirements
How does the left progression (Functional Specs → Interaction Design → Interface Design) relate to the right progression (Content Requirements → Information Architecture → Navigation Design)?

options.label: A
options.text: The left side addresses how the product works as interactive functionality (tasks/actions), while the right side addresses how the product organizes and presents information (content/navigation)

options.label: B
options.text: The left side is only for print brochures, while the right side is only for command-line tools

options.label: C
options.text: The left side ignores users completely, while the right side ignores business goals

options.label: D
options.text: Both columns represent random groupings with no logical connection across planes

questions.explanation: Functional Specifications evolve into Interaction Design (Structure) and Interface Design (Skeleton), whereas Content Requirements evolve into Information Architecture (Structure) and Navigation Design (Skeleton), before unifying in Visual Design on the Surface.
questions.hint: Follow each vertical chain upward: why does 'Functional Specifications' lead to 'Interaction Design' and 'Interface Design', while 'Content Requirements' leads to 'Information Architecture' and 'Navigation Design'?

questions.question: Why do the arrows in the 5 Elements of User Experience diagram point upward from Strategy → Scope → Structure → Skeleton → Surface?

options.label: A
options.text: Because decisions on each lower, more abstract plane constrain and inform the choices available on the higher, more concrete planes above it

options.label: B
options.text: Because designers must always pick colors and fonts on the Surface before identifying User Needs or Business Goals

options.label: C
options.text: Because the Strategy plane is the last step performed after launching the product

options.label: D
options.text: Because each plane operates in total isolation with no dependency on the others

questions.explanation: Moving from Strategy up to Surface shifts from abstract purpose to concrete sensory design; each plane depends on the decisions made in the plane beneath it.
questions.hint: Can you design a sensible navigation bar (Skeleton) or color palette (Surface) if you haven't first decided what features exist (Scope) and why users need them (Strategy)?

questions.question: In the 5 Elements of User Experience framework, Interaction Design and Information Architecture belong to the Skeleton plane, whereas Interface Design and Navigation Design belong to the Structure plane.

options.label: A
options.text: True

options.label: B
options.text: False

questions.explanation: False. Interaction Design and Information Architecture belong to the Structure plane, while Interface Design and Navigation Design belong to the Skeleton plane.
questions.hint: Check whether Information Architecture is an overarching 'Structure' concept or a screen-level 'Skeleton' wireframe concept.

questions.question: A product team writes a document listing every feature the mobile app will support and all video/article assets required, before organizing site maps or drawing wireframes. Which plane of the 5 Elements of UX is the team currently working in?

options.label: A
options.text: Scope (Functional Specifications & Content Requirements)

options.label: B
options.text: Surface (Visual Design)

options.label: C
options.text: Skeleton (Interface & Navigation Design)

options.label: D
options.text: Structure (Interaction Design & IA)

questions.explanation: Defining the list of features (Functional Specifications) and required media/text (Content Requirements) is the exact role of the Scope plane.
questions.hint: Which plane defines *what* features and content are in bounds before you design *how* they are structured?

questions.question: According to the video screenshot "7 Attributes that affect UX" (the UX Honeycomb), what are the exact seven attributes?
questions.diagram:
mindmap
  root((7 UX Attributes))
    Valuable
    Useful
    Usable
    Desirable
    Findable
    Accessible
    Credible

options.label: A
options.text: Useful, Usable, Desirable, Valuable, Findable, Accessible, and Credible

options.label: B
options.text: Fast, Cheap, Colorful, Animated, Complex, Loud, and Viral

options.label: C
options.text: Strategy, Scope, Structure, Skeleton, Surface, Closure, and Proximity

options.label: D
options.text: Tolerance, Simplicity, Visibility, Affordance, Consistency, Structure, and Feedback

questions.explanation: The 7 Attributes that affect UX shown in the honeycomb diagram are Useful, Usable, Desirable, Valuable, Findable, Accessible, and Credible.
questions.hint: Recall the seven colored hexagons in the UX Honeycomb diagram with 'Valuable' at the center.

questions.question: In the 7 Attributes that affect UX honeycomb diagram, which attribute is positioned in the central hexagon surrounded by the other six attributes?

options.label: A
options.text: Valuable

options.label: B
options.text: Findable

options.label: C
options.text: Credible

options.label: D
options.text: Accessible

questions.explanation: 'Valuable' occupies the center of the UX Honeycomb because ultimately the product must deliver value both to the users who rely on it and to the business/organization that creates it.
questions.hint: Look at the cyan hexagon right in the middle of the honeycomb—what ultimate outcome ties all six outer attributes together?

questions.question: In the 7 Attributes that affect UX, how does Useful differ from Usable?

options.label: A
options.text: Useful asks whether the product actually solves a real user problem or fulfills a need, whereas Usable asks how easy, intuitive, and error-free the product is to operate

options.label: B
options.text: Useful refers only to color contrast for screen readers, whereas Usable refers only to brand prestige

options.label: C
options.text: Usable means the product has no practical purpose, whereas Useful means buttons are hard to click

options.label: D
options.text: They mean the exact same thing and only measure server uptime

questions.explanation: A beautifully 'Usable' app that is easy to click is still a failure if it isn't 'Useful' (solving a real need); conversely, a 'Useful' tool can frustrate users if it isn't 'Usable'.
questions.hint: Imagine a flawless, easy-to-click app whose only function is to count backwards from 999—is it easy to use (Usable), or does it actually fulfill a real need (Useful)?

questions.question: A user visits a university portal and wants to download their exam schedule, but the link is buried under an unintuitive menu and search returns no results. Which of the 7 Attributes that affect UX is directly failing here?

options.label: A
options.text: Findable

options.label: B
options.text: Credible

options.label: C
options.text: Desirable

options.label: D
options.text: Valuable

questions.explanation: Findable means the product is easy to navigate and users can quickly locate the information or features they need (both externally and within the site).
questions.hint: If valuable content exists on a site, which UX attribute determines whether a user can actually locate and navigate to it?

questions.question: Compare Desirable and Credible among the 7 Attributes that affect UX:

options.label: A
options.text: Desirable focuses on emotional appeal, aesthetics, brand identity, and visual attraction, whereas Credible focuses on whether users trust and believe in the product and its information

options.label: B
options.text: Desirable means the site works with screen readers, whereas Credible means the site has a search bar

options.label: C
options.text: Credible is purely about flashy animations, whereas Desirable is about SSL certificates and privacy policies

options.label: D
options.text: Both attributes measure only how fast a database query runs

questions.explanation: Desirable captures the emotional allure created by image, identity, brand, and visual design, while Credible captures trustworthiness, security, accuracy, and authority.
questions.hint: Which attribute makes you *want* a product because of its appeal and brand, and which makes you *trust* it with your data or decisions?

questions.question: Designing a web application with proper keyboard navigation, screen-reader ARIA labels, captions for audio/video, and high color contrast for users with disabilities directly fulfills which of the 7 Attributes that affect UX?

options.label: A
options.text: Accessible

options.label: B
options.text: Credible

options.label: C
options.text: Desirable

options.label: D
options.text: Findable

questions.explanation: Accessible ensures that products and services can be used effectively by people of all abilities, including users with visual, auditory, motor, or cognitive disabilities.
questions.hint: Which attribute ensures that no user is excluded due to a disability or impairment?

questions.question: According to the 7 Attributes that affect UX, a product that is Usable (easy to operate) automatically guarantees a great overall User Experience even if it is neither Useful, Credible, nor Accessible.

options.label: A
options.text: True

options.label: B
options.text: False

questions.explanation: False. Usability is only one of the 7 attributes; a holistic UX requires moving beyond usability alone to ensure the product is also Useful, Desirable, Findable, Accessible, Credible, and Valuable.
questions.hint: Why did the video show a 7-part honeycomb instead of just a single hexagon labeled 'Usable'?

questions.question: Synthesizing the two video frameworks—how do the 5 Elements of User Experience connect to the 7 Attributes that affect UX?

options.label: A
options.text: Strategy aligns with Useful & Valuable; Structure and Skeleton (IA & Navigation) directly drive Usable & Findable; Surface (Visual Design) shapes Desirable & Credible; and Accessible spans across all planes

options.label: B
options.text: The 5 Elements apply only to hardware manufacturing, while the 7 Attributes apply only to print newspapers

options.label: C
options.text: Surface (Visual Design) is the only plane that affects Findable and Useful

options.label: D
options.text: The two frameworks contradict each other and cannot be used on the same UX project

questions.explanation: The two frameworks complement each other: Strategy grounds usefulness and value; Structure and Skeleton make content findable and interactions usable; Surface reinforces desirability and credibility; and accessibility is woven throughout.
questions.hint: Map the planes (Strategy, Structure/Skeleton, Surface) to the qualities they produce in the final user experience!

flashcards.definition: The study of how people interact with computer-based systems, encompassing design, evaluation, and implementation to make systems usable, efficient, and satisfying.
The ease with which a user can learn, use, and remember how to interact with a system to achieve their desired goals.
UI is the visual look, feel, and direct interaction controls; UX is the overall holistic experience including usability, emotions, aesthetics, and satisfaction.
The user's internal representation of how a system works based on prior knowledge and real-world experience.
The study of human information processing and decision-making applied to interactive system design to reduce mental strain and error.
1. Tolerance (error prevention/recovery), 2. Simplicity, 3. Visibility, 4. Affordance (make usage obvious), 5. Consistency, 6. Structure, 7. Feedback.
Direct Manipulation uses real-time visual feedback and physical metaphors (dragging/dropping); Batch Processing executes queued job sets without real-time user interaction.
Ubiquitous computing embeds invisible, context-aware computing in everyday environments; TUI lets users manipulate physical objects to control digital systems.
An interaction paradigm allowing users to control systems directly via brain signals without physical movement, vital for accessibility and prosthetics.
1. Make displays legible (Visual Angle), 2. Avoid absolute judgment limits, 3. Top-down processing, 4. Redundancy gain, 5. Similarity causes confusion.

flashcards.term: Mental Model Principles of Display Design
flashcards.definition: 1. Principle of Pictorial Realism (displays match real-world objects) and 2. Principle of the Moving Part (strategic motion highlights status changes).
1. Minimizing information access cost, 2. Proximity compatibility principle (group related info), 3. Principle of multiple resources (visual, auditory, tactile channels).
1. Replace memory with visual information (e.g., auto-fill), 2. Principle of predictive aiding (forecasting future states), 3. Principle of consistency.
Targets that are closer and larger take less time and precision to acquire; moving too fast toward small/distant targets causes errors (Speed-Accuracy Trade-off).
Jakob's Law: users prefer your site to work like familiar sites they already know. Hick's Law: decision time grows with the number and complexity of choices.

flashcards.term: Miller's Law, Tesler's Law & Postel's Law
flashcards.definition: Miller's: ~7±2 items in working memory. Tesler's: irreducible complexity shifts between system and user. Postel's: be liberal in what you accept, conservative in what you send.

flashcards.term: Von Restorff Effect, Peak-End Rule & Doherty Threshold
flashcards.definition: Von Restorff: distinct items stand out. Peak-End: experiences are judged by their peak and end. Doherty Threshold: <400ms response (or skeleton placeholders) keeps users engaged.
Connectedness is the strongest grouping law; Common Region overrides Proximity; Color overrides Shape in Similarity; Closure fills gaps; Figure/Ground separates focus from background.

flashcards.term: 5 Elements of User Experience (Bottom to Top)
flashcards.definition: 1. Strategy (bottom) → 2. Scope → 3. Structure → 4. Skeleton → 5. Surface (top).
The foundational bottom plane defining 'why' the product exists through Business Goals and User Needs.
The second plane defining 'what' the product builds via Functional Specifications (features) and Content Requirements (information).
The third plane defining how the system behaves and organizes data via Interaction Design and Information Architecture.
The fourth plane defining screen layout and pathways via Interface Design and Navigation Design.
The topmost plane representing Visual Design—the sensory look, typography, and colors perceived by the user.
Useful, Usable, Desirable, Valuable (center), Findable, Accessible, and Credible.
The central hexagon of the UX Honeycomb: the product must deliver meaningful value to both users and the sponsoring business.
Useful means solving a real user problem or need; Usable means the interface is easy, intuitive, and efficient to operate.
Ensuring content and features are easy to locate and navigate so users never feel lost.
Desirable evokes emotional attraction through aesthetics and brand; Credible inspires user trust and confidence in the product.
Designing products so people of all abilities—including users with visual, auditory, motor, or cognitive impairments—can use them effectively.

lectures.definition: Discipline studying the design, evaluation, and implementation of interactive computing systems for human use.
How easily a user can learn, operate, and achieve goals within a system.
The visual components and controls through which a user interacts directly with a system.
The holistic experience, emotions, and satisfaction a user has when interacting with a product.
A user's internal cognitive picture of how a system works.
Applying human information-processing psychology to reduce mental workload in interactive systems.
Affordance makes usage obvious; Tolerance prevents errors and aids recovery.
Models defining human-computer interaction (Batch, CLI, GUI, Event-Driven, Direct Manipulation, Menu, Form-Fill, Conversational, Ubiquitous, TUI, AR/VR, BCI).
Presenting information via multiple cues (e.g., color + shape + text) to improve speed and accuracy.
Placing related display information close together to support mental integration.
Distributing alerts across visual, auditory, and tactile channels to prevent sensory overload.
Display principle that forecasts future states (e.g., GPS ETA) so users can act proactively.
Closer and larger targets are faster and easier to click; governs the speed-accuracy trade-off.
Jakob's: users expect familiar conventions; Hick's: more choices increase decision time.
Postel's: accept flexible input, send clean output; Tesler's: irreducible complexity shifts from user to system.
Peak-End: memories hinge on the peak and end; Doherty: <400ms feedback keeps users in flow.
Visual perception laws (Connectedness, Common Region, Proximity, Similarity, Closure, Continuity, Common Fate, Figure/Ground).

video.definition: Layered UX model ascending from Strategy → Scope → Structure → Skeleton → Surface.
Bottom plane aligning Business Goals and User Needs.
Second plane specifying Functional Specifications and Content Requirements.
Third plane organizing system behavior and content via Interaction Design and Information Architecture.
Fourth plane arranging controls and pathways via Interface Design and Navigation Design.
Topmost plane encompassing Visual Design (colors, typography, aesthetics).
Peter Morville's UX Honeycomb: Useful, Usable, Desirable, Valuable, Findable, Accessible, and Credible.
Useful solves a genuine need; Usable makes performing tasks effortless and intuitive.
Desirable creates emotional appeal through design; Credible builds user trust and reliability.
Findable enables easy navigation; Accessible includes users of all abilities; Valuable delivers core worth to users and business.
